This report compares metaprograms generated from a single cohort across a range of k values.
Here k refers to the number of clusters specified during hierarchical clustering of spectra to define metaprograms. 

Metrics included in this notebook will be used to identify the optimal value of k for this group of samples.

## Set Up

```{r}
# helper function for plotting permutation results
# plots background points with observed values in color on top as sina plot
plot_permutation_results <- function(background_df, pvalue_df, x_axis, y_axis){
  
  ggplot(background_df, aes(x = {{ x_axis }}, y = {{ y_axis }})) +
    ggforce::geom_sina(
      color = "gray",
      alpha = 0.1
    ) +
    geom_point(
      data = pvalue_df,
      aes(
        x = {{ x_axis }},
        y = {{ y_axis }},
        color = is_significant
      ),
      size  = 3,
      shape = 18  # diamond
    ) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "red", `FALSE` = "blue")) +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90)
    )
  
}

# function to calculate the "kneedle"
# copied from https://github.com/AlexsLemonade/ews-nf/blob/main/exploratory-notebooks/05-metaprogram-correlation.Rmd
kneedle <- function(k_values, metric_values, concave = TRUE) {
  
  # Step 1: Smooth data to preserve original shape 
  fit <- smooth.spline(k_values, metric_values)
  metric_values <- predict(fit, k_values)$y
  
  # Step 2: Normalize to [0, 1]
  x <- (k_values - min(k_values)) / (max(k_values) - min(k_values))
  y <- (metric_values - min(metric_values)) / (max(metric_values) - min(metric_values))
  
  # Step 3: Subtract the diagonal (line from first to last point)
  # This "rotates" the curve so the elbow becomes a maximum
  y_diff <- y - x  # for concave (increasing); use x - y for convex (decreasing)
  if (!concave) y_diff <- x - y
  
  # Step 4: The knee is the point with the maximum difference
  knee_index <- which.max(y_diff)
  
  k_values[knee_index]
}


# function to get the max correlation of all cell scores across all mps 
# copied from inside purrr::map in exploratory notebook
# https://github.com/AlexsLemonade/ews-nf/blob/c89ff213b8bf158db0358aa7b4b95577e2e052bd/exploratory-notebooks/05-metaprogram-correlation.Rmd#L193
max_cell_score_correlation <- function(df){
  # turn df into a matrix with cells as rows and metaprograms as columns
  # the contents of the matrix are the cell scores
  mtx <- df |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(
      names_from = "metaprogram",
      values_from = "mp_score"
    ) |> 
    tidyr::unite("cell_id", unique_id, barcodes) |>
    tibble::column_to_rownames("cell_id") |> 
    as.matrix()
  
  # correlation of scores for each metaprogram 
  cor_mtx <- cor(mtx, method = "pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
  
  # get the non-self max
  diag(cor_mtx) <- 0
  max_cor_df <- data.frame(
    metaprogram = rownames(cor_mtx),
    max_correlation_cells = MatrixGenerics::rowMaxs(cor_mtx)
  )
  
  return(max_cor_df)
}

```

  purrr::map(\(file) readr::read_tsv(file, col_types = list(.default = "c", mp_score = "d")))

## Sample and patient diversity 

Metaprograms should be representative of a diverse set of samples and patients. 
This section will summarize the proportion of samples and patients found in each metaprogram. 
Any metaprograms that are only defined by a single patient will be flagged.

```{r}
# display total samples and patients
# compute this number from the proportion of samples/patients in each metaprogram
total_samples <- metrics_list |> 
  purrr::map_dbl("total_samples") |> 
  unique()

total_patients <- metrics_list |> 
  purrr::map_dbl("total_patients") |> 
  unique()

knitr::asis_output(
  glue::glue("The metaprograms explored here are comprised of **{total_samples} samples** from **{total_patients} patients**.")
)
```


### Proportion of samples 

Here each dot is a metaprogram and the value indicated is the proportion of total **samples** represented by spectra in that metaprogram. 
The dotted line indicates 10% which may help identify any metaprograms with a low representation of samples and/or patients. 

```{r}
ggplot(mp_metrics_df, aes(x = n_metaprograms, y = proportion_of_samples)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm() +
  labs(
    x = "Number of metaprograms (k)",
    y = "Proportion of total samples \n contributing to each metaprogram"
  )  +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.1, linetype = "dashed")
```

### Proportion of patients 

Here each dot is a metaprogram and the value indicated is the proportion of total **patients** represented by spectra in that metaprogram. 
Again, the dotted line indicates 10%. 

```{r}
ggplot(mp_metrics_df, aes(x = n_metaprograms, y = proportion_of_patients)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm() +
  labs(
    x = "Number of metaprograms (k)",
    y = "Proportion of total patients \n contributing to each metaprogram"
  )  +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.1, linetype = "dashed")
```

The below table reports how many metaprograms are driven by a single patient and the minimum number of patients represented in a metaprogram for a given value of k. 

```{r}
mp_metrics_df |> 
  dplyr::group_by(n_metaprograms) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    single_patient_mps = sum(num_patients == 1),
    min_num_patients_per_mp = min(num_patients),
    min_proportion_patients_per_mp = min(num_patients)/total_patients
  ) |> 
  DT::datatable(
    colnames = c("k", "Metaprograms from 1 patient", "Minimum number of patients observed in a metaprogram", "Minimum percentage of patients observed in a metaprogram")
  ) |> 
  DT::formatPercentage("min_proportion_patients_per_mp")
```

### Representation across sample types 

Here we will look at the contribution of different sample types to each of the metaprograms. 
Particularly, we will see how many of the samples are from primary, metastatic, or recurrent samples within each metaprogram. 

```{r}
disease_timing_df <- mp_metrics_df |> 
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c("num_primary_samples", "num_mets_samples", "num_recurrence_samples"),
    names_to = "sample_type", 
    values_to = "count"
  ) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    proportion = count/ num_samples,
    sample_type = stringr::word(sample_type, 2, sep = "_") |> 
      factor(labels = c("Primary", "Metastasis", "Recurrence"))
  ) |> 
  dplyr::select(n_metaprograms, metaprogram, proportion, sample_type)
```

```{r}
#| fig.height: 10
#| fig.width: 10

disease_timing_palette <- c(Primary = "#6A9FC0", Metastasis = "#C47A8A", Recurrence = "#5A9E82")

ggplot(disease_timing_df, aes(x = metaprogram, y = proportion, fill = sample_type)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(vars(n_metaprograms), scales = "free_x") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = disease_timing_palette) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  labs(
    x    = "Metaprogram",
    y    = "Proportion of samples",
    fill = "Sample type"
  ) +
  theme(
    strip.text         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position    = "top",
    axis.text.x        = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, size = 10)
  )
```


### Normalized effective sample size 

Here we will look at the normalized effective species size or Hill number of order 1. 
This is calculated by taking the exponential of Shannon's entropy and represents the effective number of common or abundant samples. 
Here we are looking for a number close to the total possible samples in that metaprogram. 
The values are normalized by the total number of samples in the metaprogram such that values close to 1 indicate all samples are equally abundant.

To determine if the observed effective sample size is not due to random chance, we performed permutation testing. 
The spectra assigned to each metaprogram were shuffled while preserving the total number of spectra assigned to each metaprogram. 
After shuffling, the normalized effective sample size was calculated to create a null distribution. 

The observed value was compared to the null distribution to get an empirical p-value, producing a single p-value for each metaprogram within a value of k.
The below plot shows both the null distribution in gray and the observed value for each metaprogram. 
The observed values are colored in red if they are significantly greater than the null distribution. 


```{r}
# pull out observations and add in significance column
neff_obs_df <- mp_metrics_df |> 
  dplyr::select(n_metaprograms, metaprogram, eff_number_norm, greater_adj_pvalue_eff_number_norm) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    is_significant = greater_adj_pvalue_eff_number_norm <= sig_value
  )

# get background for all values of k
neff_background_df <- metrics_list |> 
  purrr::map("background_mp_stats_df") |> 
  dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "n_metaprograms")
```


```{r}
#| fig.height: 15
#| fig.width: 15

plot_permutation_results(neff_background_df, neff_obs_df, metaprogram, eff_number_norm) +
  facet_wrap(vars(n_metaprograms), scale = "free_x", ncol = 3) +
  labs(
    y = "Normalized effective sample size",
    x = "Metaprogram",
    color = "significant"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_text(size = 14),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 14),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 14),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 14)
  )
```

We then can identify the percentage of metaprograms for each value of k that have a significant normalized effective sample size. 
This will be used to identify the optimal value of k in the final section. 

```{r}
neff_obs_df |> 
  dplyr::group_by(n_metaprograms) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    neff_sig_proportion = sum(is_significant)/dplyr::n()
  ) |> 
  DT::datatable(colnames = c("k", "% of metaprograms with significant effective sample size")) |> 
  DT::formatPercentage("neff_sig_proportion", 2)
```

## Correlation 

Metaprograms should be unique and non-redundant. 
Therefore we expect them to have low correlation to other metaprograms from the same value of k.

### Gene weights

Here the pairwise correlation of gene weights across all metaprograms was calculated. 
The plot then shows the maximum correlation value for each metaprogram. 
Metaprograms with a max correlation of > 0.5 are considered redundant. 
The number of metaprograms above this cutoff will be used to determine the optimal value of k. 


```{r}
correlation_df <- mp_metrics_df |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    is_passing = max_correlation <= 0.5
  )

ggplot(correlation_df, aes(x = n_metaprograms, y = max_correlation)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(aes(color = is_passing)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "red", `TRUE` = "black")) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of metaprograms (k)",
    y = "Max correlation of metaprogram gene weights",
    color = "Max correlation ≤ 0.5"
  )
```

```{r}
correlation_df |> 
  dplyr::group_by(n_metaprograms) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    num_passing_correlation = sum(is_passing),
    proportion_passing_correlation = num_passing_correlation/dplyr::n()
  ) |> 
  DT::datatable(colnames = c("k", "Number of metaprograms with max correlation ≤ 0.5", "% of metaprograms with max correlation ≤ 0.5")) |> 
  DT::formatPercentage("proportion_passing_correlation", 2)
```


### Cell scores

The gene weights for the top 200 genes are used to calculate a cell score for each cell in the dataset. 
This is done by taking the dot product of the gene weights and quantile-normalized counts in each cell. 

Here we calculate the pairwise correlation of the scores for all metaprograms to all other metaprograms in the same value of k. 
The plot below shows the max correlation observed for each metaprogram. 
Non-overlapping gene sets may have highly correlated expression.
This statistic will not be used to define the optimal value of k, as we cannot tell from this statistic alone whether the high correlation is due to the two metaprograms sharing the same set of genes or to correlated expression of the two gene sets.

```{r}
# separately calculate the correlation of metaprograms for each value of k 
# then get the max for each metaprogram and combine back into a single df for plotting
score_correlation_df <- scores_df_list |> 
  purrr::map(max_cell_score_correlation) |> 
  dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "n_metaprograms")

ggplot(score_correlation_df, aes(x = n_metaprograms, y = max_correlation_cells)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm() +
  labs(
    x = "Number of metaprograms (k)",
    y = "Max correlation of cell scores"
  )
```


## Coherence 

Metaprograms should show coherence, meaning the spectra that comprise the metaprogram are more similar to other spectra in the same metaprogram than to spectra in different metaprograms. 
To measure this, we calculated the correlation of each spectra to all other spectra. 
We then calculate the difference in medians between the distribution of correlation of spectra within a given metaprogram and between metaprograms, indicated as "coherence" throughout this report. 

Metaprograms with coherence <= 0.1 are likely to represent noise and will not be used in further analysis.

```{r}
coherence_df <- mp_metrics_df |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    is_passing = median_difference > 0.1
  )

ggplot(coherence_df, aes(x = n_metaprograms, y = median_difference)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(aes(color = is_passing)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "black")) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of metaprograms (k)",
    y = "Metaprogram coherence",
    color = "Coherence > 0.1"
  ) 

```

This plot suggests that increasing k doesn't improve metaprogram coherence after certain values of k. 
We therefore make an elbow plot showing the median coherence for each value of k and find the elbow.

```{r}
# get the median coherence for each value of k to plot
coherence_elbow_df <- mp_metrics_df |> 
  dplyr::group_by(n_metaprograms) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    median_coherence = median(median_difference)
  ) |> 
  dplyr::arrange(desc(median_coherence))
```

```{r}
ggplot(coherence_elbow_df, aes(x = n_metaprograms, median_coherence)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Number of metaprograms (k)",
    y = "Median coherence"
  )
```

We then use a modified version of the [kneedle algorithm](https://raghavan.usc.edu/papers/kneedle-simplex11.pdf) to identify the elbow. 
Here we only find one global maximum rather than a set of local maxima. 
Values of k greater than the elbow indicate no substantial gain of coherence over the lower values of k. 

```{r}
# pull out k as numeric
elbow_value <- stringr::str_remove(coherence_elbow_df$n_metaprograms, "k_") |> 
  as.numeric() |>
  kneedle(
    coherence_elbow_df$median_coherence, 
    concave = TRUE
  )

knitr::asis_output(
  glue::glue("**Value of k corresponding to the elbow: {elbow_value}**")
)
```

This plot shows the relationship of coherence with number of patients represented in a metaprogram. 
A negative correlation would suggest that metaprograms specific to a smaller subset of patients tend to have higher coherence, potentially reflecting patient-specific biological signals rather than broadly shared ones.
The R-squared shown in the plot indicates the strength of the correlation. 
The `*` indicates the slope is significantly different from zero, and the `ns` indicates the slope is not significantly different from zero.

```{r}
#| message: false

# calculate the r2 and pvalue 
patient_coherence_df <- mp_metrics_df |>
  dplyr::group_by(n_metaprograms) |>
  dplyr::summarize(
    # run lm each time since we can't store the results directly in the data frame
    r_squared = summary(lm(median_difference ~ num_patients))$r.squared,
    p_value = summary(lm(median_difference ~ num_patients))$coefficients["num_patients", "Pr(>|t|)"], 
    # identify any where the slope is significantly different from 0
    sig_label = dplyr::if_else(p_value <= sig_value, "*", "ns"),
    # make a label for the facets
    plot_label = glue::glue("R^2=='{round(r_squared, 3)} {sig_label}'")
  )

# plot the coherence x number of patients
ggplot(mp_metrics_df, aes(x = num_patients, y = median_difference)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(vars(n_metaprograms)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  geom_text(
    data = patient_coherence_df,
    aes(label = plot_label),
    x = -Inf, y = Inf,
    hjust = -0.1, vjust = 1.5,
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    parse = TRUE, # to let us show R2 properly
    size = 3
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of patients",
    y = "Coherence"
  ) + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0))
```

## Gene set specificity 

After generating metaprograms for each value of k, the top 200 genes based on gene weights were extracted from each metaprogram. 
Over-representation analysis was then run using `clusterProfiler::enricher()` function on these 200 genes.
Input gene sets include a set of custom `EWS::FLI1` activated and repressed gene sets and Hallmarks from `MSigDb`.

Any gene sets with an adjusted p value ≤ 0.05 are considered significant. 
Good metaprograms should have at least one significant gene set.

The table below shows the total number of metaprograms with zero significant gene sets for each value of k.

```{r}
mp_metrics_df |>
  dplyr::summarize(
    num_metaprograms_without_genesets = sum(num_sig_genesets == 0),
    .by = c("n_metaprograms")
  ) |> 
  DT::datatable(colnames = c("k", "Number of metaprograms with 0 significant gene sets"))
```


Metaprograms should be biologically distinct and annotated by a unique set of gene sets.
This means gene sets should be significant in as few metaprograms as possible, ideally only one metaprogram. 
For each gene set, we calculated gene set specificity using the following formula: 

$$1 - \frac{\text{# of metaprograms the gene set is significant in}- 1}{\text{total # of metaprograms} - 1}$$

A score of 1 indicates the gene set is unique to a single metaprogram, while a score of 0 indicates it is shared across all metaprograms. 

We then take the mean specificity across all gene sets and all metaprograms for a single value of k.
Metaprograms with no identified gene sets are not considered in this calculation.

To determine if this value is greater than what would be observed by random chance, we generated a null distribution by shuffling the gene sets assigned to each metaprogram, keeping the number of gene sets consistent with the observed distribution and recalculating the mean specificity. 
The gene sets were also weighted by the number of times they were observed.

The below plot shows the observed mean gene set specificity and the associated background distribution for each value of k. 
Any values of k with a significant mean gene set specificity are indicated in red.

```{r}
# pull out observations and summarize to get the mean for each value of k
gss_obs_df <- mp_metrics_df |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    overall_geneset_specificity = mean(mean_geneset_specificity, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = c("n_metaprograms")
  )

# get background mean gene expression for each k and each replicate
gss_background_df <- metrics_list |> 
  purrr::map("background_specificity_df") |> 
  dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "n_metaprograms") |> 
  # overall_geneset_specificity is per k
  dplyr::select(n_metaprograms, replicate, overall_geneset_specificity) |> 
  unique()

# pull out the number of replicates 
# note this isn't stored as a number in the objects 
nreps <- max(gss_background_df$replicate |> as.numeric())

# join observed values with background values
# here we are calculating the overall mean pvalue so that we get one pvalue for each k
# this mirrors what we did in: https://github.com/AlexsLemonade/ews-nf/blob/main/exploratory-notebooks/06-gene-set-uniqueness.Rmd
# the metrics calculation script calculates per mp so we need to do this separately here
pvalue_df <- gss_background_df |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    dplyr::rename(gss_obs_df, obs_value = overall_geneset_specificity),
    by = c("n_metaprograms")
  ) |>
  # indicator column for if background >= observation
  dplyr::mutate(greater_than_obs = overall_geneset_specificity >= obs_value,
                less_than_obs = overall_geneset_specificity <= obs_value) |>
  dplyr::summarize(
      overall_geneset_specificity = unique(obs_value),
      # we see values that are both higher and lower so use a two-tailed test
      p_greater = (sum(greater_than_obs) + 1) / (nreps + 1),
      p_lower = (sum(less_than_obs) + 1) / (nreps + 1),
      overall_geneset_specificity_pvalue = min(p_greater, p_lower) * 2,
      .by = c("n_metaprograms")
    ) |>
    # add in adjusted pvalue
    dplyr::mutate(
      overall_geneset_specificity_adj_pvalue = p.adjust(overall_geneset_specificity_pvalue, method = "BH"),
      is_significant = overall_geneset_specificity_pvalue <= sig_value
    )
```


```{r}
plot_permutation_results(gss_background_df, pvalue_df, n_metaprograms, overall_geneset_specificity) +
  labs(
    y = "Mean gene set specificity",
    x = "Metaprogram",
    color = "significant"
  ) 
```
